candidates.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
candidates.description: A leader positioned vertically above another leader is judged as more powerful than a leader positioned at the same vertical level.
candidates.citation_sentence: As a part of this approach, we (Giessner & Schubert, 2007) conducted a series of experiments examining whether the vertical spatial dimension relates to power perceptions of leaders.
candidates.notes: Study 2 introduced a modified paradigm to separate vertical rank order from magnitude of elevation. The rank-order effect was significant and the authors explicitly conclude that rank order matters; this effect was not isolated in the original Study 1a paradigm.

candidates.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
candidates.description: Describing a leader as powerful rather than powerless causes participants to place the leader's box higher in an organization chart.
candidates.citation_sentence: In Study 3a of the same original paper (Giessner & Schubert, 2007), we had tested the reverse effect -namely whether describing a leader as powerful versus powerless would result in placing a box of this leader on a higher versus lower vertical position within an organization chart.
candidates.notes: Study 1 of the current paper replicates original Study 3a. The authors explicitly state that the study successfully replicated the main findings. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.original_title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders' power are interrelated
candidates.description: A greater magnitude of vertical elevation between a leader and subordinates causes the leader to be judged as more powerful, even when hierarchical rank remains unchanged.
candidates.citation_sentence: As a part of this approach, we (Giessner & Schubert, 2007) conducted a series of experiments examining whether the vertical spatial dimension relates to power perceptions of leaders.
candidates.notes: Study 2 directly follows up on original Study 1a's magnitude-of-elevation claim. The current study found no magnitude effect, and the authors describe the original positive finding as a false positive. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

prior_source_review.finding: The matched descriptions target Study 1 (power to placement). Study 2 reverses the causal direction and is not interchangeable even though the original DOI is shared. A genuine type disagreement remains for Study 1.
